summary: Defines the terminology used when discussing SPEERMINT, which concerns how voice and multimedia providers connect with each other over IP. It is a shared vocabulary so that related documents use words consistently.

eli5.summary: When people work on a project together, they need to use the same words for the same things. This note is the word list for connecting phone and video services between companies.

questions: what is a federation in speermint
subtitle: Vocabulary for connecting voice and video services between different providers.

tldr.problem: Voice and multimedia providers need a common vocabulary when describing how their networks interconnect and route calls to each other, but the term 'peering' was historically used inconsistently to describe connections at different protocol layers.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines precise terms for session-layer peering (connecting at the SIP signaling level), distinguishes direct from indirect peering, describes peering functions (signaling, media, routing), and introduces the concept of peering federations.
tldr.outcome: Operators and architects have standard terminology for discussing VoIP interconnection, enabling clearer specifications, implementations, and service agreements.

facts.label: Primary use case
facts.value: VoIP interconnection (also applicable to multimedia/real-time communications)

today: RFC 5486 is Informational and remains the standard terminology reference for SPEERMINT work. The SPEERMINT working group used this vocabulary in subsequent RFCs defining session peering protocols and best practices.

sections.title: Why Terminology Matters for Peering
sections.content:
SPEERMINT stands for Session PEERing for Multimedia INTerconnect, a working group focused on how independent voice and multimedia service providers connect their networks to exchange calls. The term 'VoIP peering' had been used for many interconnection practices, but the vocabulary was vague and inconsistent. Peering could refer to agreement-based commercial relationships, or to technical connections at different layers of the network stack.

This document establishes clear terminology focused on layer 5 peering (the session layer where SIP signaling occurs), distinct from layer 3 peering (the IP routing layer). Most of the SPEERMINT work addresses session-layer interconnection, although the document acknowledges that both layers matter and that some organizations undertake both simultaneously.
sections.eli5: Phone companies used to call any kind of connection 'peering,' but that was confusing. This document separates 'peering' at the SIP level (where phone calls are set up) from 'peering' at the IP routing level (where packets are sent). Most voice peering is at the SIP level.

sections.title: Core Concepts and Components
sections.content:
Several fundamental elements appear in every peering discussion. A Session Establishment Data (SED) set is the collection of parameters needed to route a call to the correct destination SIP server, including the target SIP URI, the server's fully-qualified domain name (FQDN), port and transport protocol, and security parameters like which TLS certificate to present. A Signaling Path Border Element (SBE) is the gateway device on the boundary of a domain that handles SIP signaling between domains; it typically provides protocol translation (e.g., H.323 to SIP), hides internal topology, and enforces admission control. A Data Path Border Element (DBE) is the equivalent component for media (the actual voice data), providing media relay, firewall traversal, and sometimes deep packet inspection.

The PSTN (Public Switched Telephone Network) is the traditional circuit-switched telephone system, whereas an IP path is simply one or more IP routers. A Peer Network is the set of SIP user agents (endpoints) in a single administrative domain that can be reached via some IP path. A Service Provider (SP) offers layer 3 transport (e.g., Ethernet, VPN, Frame Relay), while a SIP Service Provider (SSP), also called an Internet Telephony Service Provider (ITSP), offers session services using SIP. An SSP may control both signaling (SBE) and media (DBE) or just one of them.
sections.eli5: An SBE is the guy at the border who passes phone call setup messages from one company's SIP servers to another's. A DBE passes the actual voice. SED is the address book entry for where to send calls to the other company. An SP is a basic internet provider; an SSP is a phone/video company using SIP.

sections.title: Forms of Peering
sections.content:
Layer 3 peering connects two service providers' IP networks so they can exchange IP packets destined for each other. It uses routing protocols like BGP and is generally agnostic to what kind of traffic the packets carry. Layer 5 peering (session peering) connects two SSPs' SIP servers for the purpose of routing call signaling between their customers, without restricting how media packets flow.

Direct peering is a bilateral connection between two SSPs without an intervening layer 5 network. Indirect peering (or transit peering) routes traffic through one or more transit providers. Static peering requires prior agreement and configuration before any calls can pass; an example is a federation (see below). On-demand peering allows two SSPs to exchange calls without pre-configuration, using dynamic discovery mechanisms to learn routing information at call time.
sections.eli5: Layer 3 is IP routers talking to IP routers (how packets move). Layer 5 is SIP servers talking to SIP servers (how calls get set up). Direct is two companies connected. Indirect is using a middle company. Static means you have to set up the connection beforehand. On-demand means you figure it out when a call arrives.

sections.title: Functions Required for Peering
sections.content:
Four core functions support peering operations. The Signaling Function (SF) routes SIP requests to establish and maintain calls and assists in discovering parameters for the Media Function. Any SIP processing element (proxy, SBE, or user agent) can perform this. The Media Function (MF) handles media-related operations such as transcoding (converting between different audio codecs) and media security, typically performed by media endpoints like DBEs or user agents.

The Look-Up Function (LUF) determines which domain should receive a request, for example by translating a phone number to a SIP URI via ENUM, or by querying a SIP proxy for redirection. The Location Routing Function (LRF) determines where in a domain to send the request—it takes the target domain name and discovers the actual SIP server address and other routing information. These functions may be performed by the SSP itself or by a third party, and the SPEERMINT work focuses on how to make them work across domain boundaries.
sections.eli5: Signaling Function: route the call setup messages to the right SIP server. Media Function: make sure the voice works (maybe convert the audio format). Look-Up Function: turn a phone number into a SIP address. Location Routing Function: find the actual SIP server for that address.

sections.title: Federations and Governance
sections.content:
A federation is a group of SSPs that mutually agree to exchange calls using SIP and establish a common set of administrative and technical rules. Examples of federation rules include using a common domain name for all members, requiring certain audio codecs (like G.711), mandating authentication methods (like TLS), specifying transport protocols (like TCP), and defining address resolution mechanisms (like ENUM). Federations provide static peering with contractual and technical governance: participants cannot just send calls whenever they want; they must be pre-approved members following the federation's rules.

An important note: an SSP can be part of no federation (using only bilateral peering agreements), part of a single federation, or part of multiple federations simultaneously. The same SSP can mix bilateral and federated peers. This flexibility allows operators to start with bilateral agreements and later join federations if benefits arise, or to participate in multiple specialized federations for different customer types or geographies.
sections.eli5: A federation is a club of phone companies that promise to use the same rules when calling each other—same codecs, same security, same domain names. You can be in zero clubs, one club, or many clubs at once. You can also make bilateral deals with specific companies.
